His requests that are still live:

Let me choose the options."    - "anything left for me to decide?" (answered; the open decisions have since changed, see section 8).

Ours: reported once through `report_unexpected_error` at the top of an entry point, the person sees "Something went wrong on our side", work stops, no handling code. A service the person chose failing: told truthfully, not reported. Cannot be told: comes to us. "Two causes that leave the person doing the same thing share one sentence." "A status code, an exception type, or the way the failure arrives … is not a cause." Never record a failure as a success. Tool-call exception: a failed AI tool call is shown in the turn, error goes to the model, reported only with automatic reports on.

The session fixing misdirected failures reported that every place on the list was done. I had two independent reviewers read its changes against the error-handling rules, and the work is not ready to land. They found 31 problems, three of them serious. The session is now working through them, and nothing is committed.

## The three serious problems

- **Lost work.** After a save fails because of a bug of ours, autosave stops until the app restarts. The header can still say "Saved" while later edits are not saved.
- **The app may end on a menu click.** A failed export or open from the File menu now throws an error with nothing above it to catch and report it. This was read in the code, not run.
- **Free replies.** On the server, the charge for a reply can be given back after the reply was delivered, by sending the same turn again with a request that fails.

## What went wrong

Most findings are two mistakes the rules already warn about.

- **Deciding by the kind of error, not its cause.** One check looks at four system error numbers and is applied to everything. A disk quota or an unplugged drive is then called our fault.
- **Swinging to "our side".** A browser tab whose sign-in ended, a file name typed without ".3mf", and a Windows computer without WebView2 all showed "Something went wrong on our side" and filed a report.

One of these was mine. I told the session that every error answer from GitHub during the update check is ours. An office that shares one address hits GitHub's limit, and each person there would get a report dialog at every launch. I have corrected it.

## What I settled from the rules

- Autosave keeps trying after a failure of ours and reports it once.
- A browser that is no longer signed in at checkout is the person's and is not reported.
- A turn is not charged when no answer reached the person.
- Four of the session's five questions and four of its six sentences are answered or withdrawn. Two of those sentences were for failures nobody has made happen.

**One change you should know about.** Deleting an account now stops with "Something went wrong on our side" when Chargebee cannot find the subscription. Before, the account was deleted. I kept this, because deleting could leave a card being charged with no account to cancel from. The report names the account so we can end the subscription by hand.

## Decision needed: two sentences

Both are sentences we write for the person, and neither is built.

- **A chat that is too long.** Today: "The request was too large for the OpenAI service." My pick: "This chat is too long for OpenAI. Start a new chat, or send fewer pictures."
- **A project open in another JusPrin window.** This can happen when two copies of JusPrin run at once. Today: "The project couldn't be opened. Try again." My pick: "This project is open in another JusPrin window. Close it there, then try again."

## Decision needed: one addition to an OrcaSlicer file

When our server fails during browser sign-in, the app says "Signing in didn't finish" and we never hear of it. The app cannot tell this from the person pressing Cancel, because OrcaSlicer's sign-in code passes on only a translated message. Adding one field that says which step failed would fix it. It is yours because that file is OrcaSlicer's and every upstream merge carries the change. Without it, we hear of these failures only when our server itself reports them. My pick is to add it. Should I?

Do you approve the two sentences: approve both, or different wording?
What the fuck is going on?

content.text:
Yes, that is fair, and it explains most of what went wrong. Each of the 42 places needs one decision: whose failure is it. Once that is decided, the code change is small, because both ways of handling a failure already exist in the app.

- **The person's failure, or their service's:** an if/else that shows the other side's words in the frame you approved (`OpenRouter says: "…"`), and the app carries on.
- **Ours:** remove the catch or the default value, so the failure travels up to the handler that already reports it and shows "Something went wrong on our side".

Neither needs new machinery. The session built some anyway, and I let it. By my count from the two reviews, about a dozen of the 31 problems sit in code that should not exist:

- a general sorter that decides whose failure it is from four system error numbers;
- a "stop autosave for the rest of the run" state;
- bookkeeping for giving a charge back;
- a failed "Save preset" click that starts an AI turn.

About ten more are the decision itself made wrongly, such as calling a file name typed without ".3mf" our fault. Those are the real mistakes. They were hard to see because they were buried in 2,600 changed lines, where a one-line decision per place would have shown them.

**Where it is not purely mechanical**

- **Removing a catch is only safe if a reporting handler sits above it.** The File menu has none, which is why a failed export may now end the app. Adding one handler at an entry point is still a small change, but it has to be checked for each place.
- **Three of the places are not about who gets the failure.** They are separate jobs and should not ride in this change:
  - giving the charge back when a reply fails on our side;
  - bringing back a project that disappears after an interrupted chat restore;
  - telling a Cancel during browser sign-in apart from our server failing.

**What I propose**

1. Stop the session from patching its large change.
2. Write one line per place: whose failure it is, and which mechanical change follows. You can check that list in a few minutes, before any code is written.
3. Make the changes from that list, small enough to review one by one. Where the current change already has the right small piece, such as the frame for a service's words, I reuse it.

# Handoff: failures that still go to the wrong one (written 2026-11-25)

STATUS OF THIS FILE: draft. The 17 simple changes described under "What is done" are still being
made. That section is filled in when they land.

This is a working note for whoever continues the error-handling work in JusPrin 2 (this repository)
and its server (`/Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise`, folder `web_ent/jusprin/`). It is not
committed and must stay untracked.

## What this work is

The rule is the "Error handling" section of `AGENTS.md` here and of `CLAUDE.md` in tsd-enterprise.
Read it first. In one sentence: each failure has someone who can do something about it, and error
handling is getting the failure to them in a form they can use.

In November 2026 three code readers, given only that rule, listed places where the app or the
server sends a failure to the wrong one. The list is `error-handling-misrouted-failures.md` in this
checkout (untracked). It has 42 entries; three of them hold several places each, so there are 50
places.

## How Kenneth wants it done

His words, 2026-11-25:

> the changes should be very mechanical. There shouldn't be anything fancy about those so-called
> fixes, because you really just do some try/catch, if/else, or remove them. For situations like
> these, the most important decision is about whether or not you want to handle, and not about how
> you handle

> for each of the sites that was already identified, check to see if it can be patched with simple
> mechanism. for any of the sites, If it needs anything fancy, report back.

So, for each place:

1. Decide whose failure it is. That is the whole decision. Look at what the other side really
   says, not at a status code or an error number.
2. Make the failure happen first in the real app or on the real local server. His standing rule:
   "Never apply a fix for a bug you cannot reproduce." A unit test with a fake is not enough.
   34 of the 50 places had never been made to happen when this note was written.
3. If the change is an added or removed try/catch or if/else, or deleted handling, make it.
4. If it needs anything more, do not build it. Tell Kenneth what is missing and wait for his word.

## What went wrong the first time

One session was given all 42 entries at once. It changed about 120 files and reported everything
done. Two independent reviews found 31 problems, three of them worse than what the change set out
to fix: edits lost while the header said "Saved", a File menu click that could end the app, and a
reply that could be had without paying. Kenneth had all of it reversed. The mistakes to avoid:

- Deciding by the kind of error. The change had one shared check that looked at four system error
  numbers and was applied to every failure. The rule says a status code, an exception type or the
  way a failure arrives is not a cause. Decide at the place that knows what it was doing.
- Swinging to "ours". A browser tab whose sign-in ended, a file name typed without ".3mf", GitHub
  limiting an office's shared address: each was shown as "Something went wrong on our side" and
  reported. Ask of every branch you make ours: can a person get here by doing something ordinary?
- Throwing with nothing above to report it. Before a failure is made ours, walk up from the throw
  to the entry point on every path and name the handler that reports it. If there is none,
  OrcaSlicer's last handler rethrows and the app may end.
- Building machinery. "Stop autosave for the rest of the run", bookkeeping for refunds, a failed
  button press that started an AI turn. None of it was asked for.
- Too many questions to Kenneth. Answer a question from the rule first. Bring him only what the
  rule leaves open, said as what a person sees, never by a label or a number.

The reversed work is kept for reference only in two patch files (see "Where things are"). Do not
apply them.

- The message after the app's 120-second limit on a reply: "Don't need to fix this one. This error

- A credit pack paid by a method that clears later: "we will only take credit cards. ignore this".
